xQDr05DvYqU.overview: Fracture mechanisms — an explanatory companion to the matched source presentation.

sections.heading: Foundation
paragraphs: Bone breaks when applied stress exceeds its strength. The same force can fracture weak bone while leaving stronger bone intact. Understanding loading explains patterns but must be combined with age, bone quality and clinical history.

sections.heading: How it develops
paragraphs: Bending places one surface in tension and the opposite in compression. Torsion can create spiral patterns, while axial loading may produce impaction or articular compression. Direct blows often cause injury near the contact point.

sections.heading: Recognizing the pattern
paragraphs: Muscle or ligament traction can avulse an attachment fragment. In children, the physis may fail where an adult would sustain a ligament injury. The weakest structure in the system determines the injury pattern.

sections.heading: Clinical reasoning
paragraphs: Repetitive submaximal loading can accumulate microdamage and cause stress injury. A sudden training increase or impaired repair capacity shifts the balance toward failure. This mechanism differs from a single major traumatic event.

sections.heading: Avoiding mistakes
paragraphs: Mechanism guides the search for associated injury but should not be treated as forensic certainty. High-energy fractures require attention to soft tissues and other body regions. A low-energy fracture may indicate a need for bone-health assessment.

D7WUwKID7d0.overview: Nutrition and fracture healing — learn the anatomical reason behind the key distinctions.

sections.heading: Core concept
paragraphs: Fracture repair requires energy, protein and micronutrients, but no single ordinary food inevitably prevents union. Interpret a list of foods through dietary patterns, intake and underlying health rather than assuming a universal prohibited-food rule.

sections.heading: First distinction
paragraphs: Insufficient energy or protein can limit repair. Calcium and vitamin D support skeletal health, but increasing supplements beyond need does not guarantee faster healing. Deficiencies and restricted diets may require individualized assessment.

sections.heading: Second distinction
paragraphs: Excessive alcohol and smoking are relevant recovery risks; smoking is not a food but can impair healing through vascular and biological effects. Highly restrictive diets can also be counterproductive if they reduce adequate nutrition during recovery.

sections.heading: Clinical application
paragraphs: Claims about caffeine, salt or processed foods should consider dose and the overall diet. An association with poor bone health is not proof that one serving will delay a particular fracture. Medication decisions should not be changed based on a food list.

sections.heading: Pitfalls and follow-up
paragraphs: Stable treatment, infection control, circulation and follow-up remain essential. A balanced diet supports these measures but cannot correct unstable fixation or an infected nonunion. Discuss nutritional concerns with the treating team rather than relying on miracle foods.

NX3bxNPzqTM.overview: Supporting fracture healing — learn the anatomical reason behind the key distinctions.

sections.heading: Core concept
paragraphs: Healing requires a suitable mechanical environment and viable tissue. Helpful actions support normal repair; they do not guarantee a shorter timetable for every fracture. Location, injury severity and patient health create substantial variation.

sections.heading: First distinction
paragraphs: Follow the prescribed protection and loading plan. Too much movement at an unstable site can impair repair, while appropriate movement of safe joints helps preserve function. Pain improvement alone does not establish sufficient union for heavy loading.

sections.heading: Second distinction
paragraphs: Adequate calories, protein and relevant micronutrients support repair. Identify deficiency rather than assuming large supplement doses are beneficial. Smoking cessation and avoiding excessive alcohol improve the overall recovery environment.

sections.heading: Clinical application
paragraphs: Attend follow-up to assess alignment and progress. Persistent pain, wound drainage or an unexpected plateau needs reassessment for mechanical or biological problems. Treatments marketed as stimulators are not universally indicated or guaranteed effective.

sections.heading: Pitfalls and follow-up
paragraphs: The practical goal is uncomplicated union and restored function. Rehabilitation, falls prevention and management of diabetes or bone fragility may matter more than an unproven shortcut. Changes to medicines or supplements should be discussed with the treating clinician.

Lk1CBijkKJQ.overview: Shoulder and arm trauma course introduction — learn the anatomical reason behind the key distinctions.

sections.heading: Core concept
paragraphs: The shoulder girdle connects the upper limb to the trunk through the clavicle, scapula and humerus. Its large movement range depends on coordinated joints and muscles. This mobility helps explain why instability and tendon injury accompany trauma.

sections.heading: First distinction
paragraphs: Study clavicle and scapula injuries before the proximal humerus and dislocations. Relating each fracture to surrounding nerves, vessels and muscle attachments makes the injury patterns easier to remember than isolated eponyms.

sections.heading: Second distinction
paragraphs: For every case, identify mechanism, anatomical structure, skin integrity and neurovascular status. Then examine orthogonal images for alignment and associated fractures. A single painful point does not define the whole injury.

sections.heading: Clinical application
paragraphs: Management principles balance stability, tissue preservation and rehabilitation. A younger athlete with recurrent instability poses a different problem from a frail older adult with a fragility fracture. Patient goals influence the meaning of a successful result.

sections.heading: Pitfalls and follow-up
paragraphs: Use this introduction as a route through the course rather than a substitute for each detailed lecture. Revisit normal anatomy when a classification becomes confusing, and connect complications to the structure that was damaged.

g9GM06BiySc.overview: Orthopedic trauma foundations — learn the anatomical reason behind the key distinctions.

sections.heading: Core concept
paragraphs: Orthopedic trauma combines the mechanical problem of disrupted structure with the biological problem of tissue repair. A fracture description explains the injury; a whole-patient assessment determines its urgency and the safest treatment priorities.

sections.heading: First distinction
paragraphs: Begin with mechanism, pattern and displacement, then learn healing biology. These ideas explain why two similar-looking fractures may have different stability or healing potential. Soft-tissue injury is as important as the visible bone line.

sections.heading: Second distinction
paragraphs: Assessment includes skin, circulation, nerve function and adjacent joints. Imaging adds information about alignment and morphology, but does not replace serial examination. Life-threatening injuries take priority before definitive fracture management.

sections.heading: Clinical application
paragraphs: Treatment can be organized as restoring alignment, maintaining stability and recovering function. The chosen methods depend on site, age, biology, patient condition and goals. Open injury adds contamination and tissue-coverage considerations.

sections.heading: Pitfalls and follow-up
paragraphs: Complications can arise early, such as vascular injury or compartment syndrome, or later, such as nonunion and stiffness. Learn the mechanism of each complication so that follow-up becomes purposeful rather than a checklist of names.

7VzcxT1T-lM.overview: Odontoid fracture classification — learn the anatomical reason behind the key distinctions.

sections.heading: Core concept
paragraphs: The dens projects from C2 and participates in atlantoaxial stability. Injury can threaten spinal stability and neurological structures. Cervical trauma assessment and protection require trained care, not self-testing of neck motion.

sections.heading: First distinction
paragraphs: Anderson-DAlonzo type I affects the tip, type II the base, and type III extends into the C2 body. Location influences healing because the base has less favorable biological and mechanical conditions than the cancellous body.

sections.heading: Second distinction
paragraphs: CT defines the bony pattern and displacement. Neurological findings and possible ligament injury may require further assessment. A seemingly small type I fragment may accompany a more complex upper-cervical injury, so context remains important.

sections.heading: Clinical application
paragraphs: Management considers displacement, stability, age, bone quality, neurological status and overall health. Some injuries are immobilized and others stabilized surgically. The classification alone is insufficient to select one treatment for all patients.

sections.heading: Pitfalls and follow-up
paragraphs: Type II fractures are particularly associated with nonunion. Treatment in older adults balances healing, stability and the burdens of immobilization or surgery. Follow-up must assess symptoms and stability rather than assuming a classification guarantees an outcome.

J3_iSJY8r7A.overview: Salter-Harris classification — learn the anatomical reason behind the key distinctions.

sections.heading: Core concept
paragraphs: The growth plate separates epiphysis and metaphysis in a growing bone. Damage can alter future length or alignment. Classifying the path through these structures helps connect the radiograph to growth and joint consequences.

sections.heading: First distinction
paragraphs: Type I crosses the physis and type II exits into metaphysis. Type II can leave a triangular metaphyseal fragment. These patterns may spare the joint surface, but prognosis still depends on location, displacement and the degree of physeal injury.

sections.heading: Second distinction
paragraphs: Type III passes from physis into epiphysis and joint; type IV crosses metaphysis, physis and epiphysis. Both require attention to articular congruity and growth-plate alignment. Type V is a compression injury and may be initially occult.

sections.heading: Clinical application
paragraphs: A normal film does not exclude a clinically important physeal injury. Treatment and follow-up are site-specific, and careful technique is required when reduction is needed. Growth surveillance may continue after the fracture itself has healed.

sections.heading: Pitfalls and follow-up
paragraphs: Do not use the number alone as a severity scale that predicts every outcome. Remaining growth, blood supply and exact site matter. Later asymmetry or angular deformity can reveal growth arrest that was not evident during initial recovery.

pJM7PDwyL0A.overview: Danis-Weber ankle classification — learn the anatomical reason behind the key distinctions.

sections.heading: Core concept
paragraphs: The distal tibiofibular syndesmosis links the tibia and fibula above the ankle joint. Weber classification describes fibular fracture level relative to this structure. It is a useful starting point but not a complete ankle-stability assessment.

sections.heading: First distinction
paragraphs: Weber A lies below the syndesmosis, B at its level and C above it. Higher fractures often raise concern for syndesmotic disruption, but the medial structures and associated fractures determine the full pattern.

sections.heading: Second distinction
paragraphs: Inspect the ankle mortise, medial clear space, talar alignment and posterior malleolus. Examination of the proximal fibula is important when the mechanism suggests a Maisonneuve injury. An ankle-only image may miss the proximal component.

sections.heading: Clinical application
paragraphs: Stability guides management more directly than the letter alone. Weight-bearing or other specialist-selected imaging can help in uncertain patterns. Treatment restores a congruent mortise and addresses instability where present.

sections.heading: Pitfalls and follow-up
paragraphs: Do not assume every Weber B injury is unstable or every low fracture is harmless. Deltoid ligament injury and medial malleolar involvement can change the assessment. Classify the fibula, then evaluate the whole ankle ring.

LI-c_eBJGBM.overview: Schatzker tibial plateau classification — learn the anatomical reason behind the key distinctions.

sections.heading: Core concept
paragraphs: The tibial plateau bears knee load and supports joint congruity. Fractures may split, depress or separate the articular surface, often with meniscal or ligament injury. Soft-tissue condition influences management as much as the bony pattern.

sections.heading: First distinction
paragraphs: Types I, II and III describe lateral split, lateral split-depression and lateral depression respectively. The distinction explains whether fragments are separated, pushed downward, or both, and helps identify the reconstruction problem.

sections.heading: Second distinction
paragraphs: Type IV involves the medial plateau, V both plateaus, and VI includes metaphyseal-diaphyseal dissociation. Complex patterns can signal substantial energy and instability. The classification does not fully describe every posterior fragment.

sections.heading: Clinical application
paragraphs: Radiographs establish the injury and CT clarifies articular geometry. Check vascular and nerve status and monitor for compartment syndrome. Selected MRI may answer soft-tissue questions; it is not a replacement for urgent clinical assessment.

sections.heading: Pitfalls and follow-up
paragraphs: Treatment aims to preserve alignment, joint congruity and stability while respecting swollen soft tissues. Long-term problems include stiffness, malalignment and post-traumatic arthritis. The type number helps communication but cannot alone dictate timing or fixation strategy.

rJTSNkk_uvg.overview: Intertrochanteric fracture stability — learn the anatomical reason behind the key distinctions.

sections.heading: Core concept
paragraphs: Intertrochanteric fractures lie outside the hip capsule between the trochanters. Stability depends on the ability of the reconstructed fragments to resist loading, particularly the integrity of supporting cortices and the lateral wall.

sections.heading: First distinction
paragraphs: Evans-Jensen descriptions distinguish simple two-part patterns from more fragmented injuries with loss of support. Greater or lesser trochanteric fragments can indicate disruption of different stabilizing regions. Systems and modifications differ, so specify which version is used.

sections.heading: Second distinction
paragraphs: Reverse-obliquity and certain subtrochanteric extensions behave differently from a standard intertrochanteric line. Describe these features explicitly instead of relying on a category label. Imaging should include the full pattern and assess displacement.

sections.heading: Clinical application
paragraphs: Treatment commonly uses operative stabilization with construct selection based on pattern, bone quality and patient condition. Perioperative care also addresses pain, medical optimization, mobilization and prevention of complications in often frail patients.

sections.heading: Pitfalls and follow-up
paragraphs: A fracture that looks reduced may still lack structural support. Mechanical stability, not the number of visible pieces alone, explains failure risk. Subsequent care should include osteoporosis and falls assessment when the injury followed low-energy trauma.

ay9sAvwxino.overview: Garden femoral-neck classification — learn the anatomical reason behind the key distinctions.

sections.heading: Core concept
paragraphs: Femoral-neck fractures are intracapsular and can disrupt blood supply to the head. Displacement therefore affects both mechanics and biological viability. The Garden system primarily describes alignment on the AP image.

sections.heading: First distinction
paragraphs: Type I is incomplete or valgus-impacted and type II complete but nondisplaced. These are often grouped as nondisplaced for practical discussion, but lateral tilt and other features may still influence stability and treatment planning.

sections.heading: Second distinction
paragraphs: Type III is partially displaced and type IV completely displaced. The categories have imperfect observer agreement, so describe the visible displacement rather than treating classification as a perfectly reproducible measurement.

sections.heading: Clinical application
paragraphs: Treatment considers age, physiological reserve, activity, bone quality and the feasibility of preserving the head. Fixation and arthroplasty address different circumstances. A category is not sufficient to choose a procedure without patient-specific assessment.

sections.heading: Pitfalls and follow-up
paragraphs: Osteonecrosis and nonunion are important concerns. Persistent hip pain after a fall may warrant further imaging even when initial radiographs are normal. A low-energy hip fracture also requires coordinated rehabilitation, bone-health and falls-prevention care.

F4FzJ2HcFSg.overview: Posterior hip dislocation classification — learn the anatomical reason behind the key distinctions.

sections.heading: Core concept
paragraphs: A posterior hip dislocation displaces the femoral head behind the acetabulum, often after substantial trauma. The sciatic nerve and femoral-head blood supply are at risk. Associated fractures influence stability and definitive management.

sections.heading: First distinction
paragraphs: The Thompson-Epstein system distinguishes a simple dislocation from patterns with posterior acetabular rim injury, comminution, acetabular-floor injury or femoral-head fracture. The associated bony damage is the essential concept behind the categories.

sections.heading: Second distinction
paragraphs: Examination documents limb position and distal nerve and vascular function. Radiographs confirm direction and fractures; post-treatment CT commonly assesses congruity, fragments and occult associated injuries. The entire trauma context must be considered.

sections.heading: Clinical application
paragraphs: Urgent clinician-led reduction aims to restore congruity and reduce ongoing tissue compromise. These notes do not provide a self-reduction technique. Associated fractures, instability or incarcerated fragments may require further operative care.

sections.heading: Pitfalls and follow-up
paragraphs: Osteonecrosis, sciatic nerve injury and post-traumatic arthritis can occur despite initial reduction. Continued follow-up is needed. Do not confuse this system for posterior dislocations with Pipkin classification, which specifically describes femoral-head fractures.

lDS-uGbi8Xk.overview: Pipkin femoral-head classification — learn the anatomical reason behind the key distinctions.

sections.heading: Core concept
paragraphs: Femoral-head fractures often accompany hip dislocation and affect an articular surface essential for load transmission. Classification considers the fracture relative to the fovea and associated femoral-neck or acetabular injury.

sections.heading: First distinction
paragraphs: Type I is below the fovea and type II above it, involving the more important weight-bearing portion. This anatomical distinction helps explain why fragment location matters in addition to fragment size and displacement.

sections.heading: Second distinction
paragraphs: Type III combines a type I or II head fracture with a femoral-neck fracture. Type IV combines a head fracture with an acetabular fracture. The associated injury can dominate prognosis and management.

sections.heading: Clinical application
paragraphs: Imaging assesses joint congruity, fragments and associated fractures, often using CT after urgent clinical management of dislocation. Neurovascular assessment and whole-patient trauma evaluation remain essential before focusing on the classification.

sections.heading: Pitfalls and follow-up
paragraphs: Management aims to restore a stable congruent joint while considering head viability and associated damage. Osteonecrosis, arthritis and heterotopic ossification are potential complications. The type is a communication tool rather than a complete treatment algorithm.
